why.correct: The pictures show the quartered center-of-mass symbol on one straight dashed line, equally spaced every 0.20 s. Nothing outside the wrench pushes it sideways along the slippery ice, so its center of mass keeps a constant velocity even while the wrench turns.
options: Right: the center of mass moves like a single point object that nothing pushes or pulls along the ice.
The handle end follows a wavy path because it swings around the center of mass; the center of mass itself stays on the dashed line.
The dashed line through the five positions is straight; the head turning around the center of mass does not bend that path.
The spacing between positions is the same every 0.20 s, so the center of mass is not speeding up.

why.correct: Average speed = distance ÷ time = 2.4 m ÷ 0.80 s = 3.0 m/s.

The handle end swings around the center of mass while the whole wrench slides, so its displacement in each interval keeps changing in size and direction. That is why the center of mass, not any one point of the object, is the point that moves simply.
options: Right: the handle end combines the steady slide with the turning, so its steps are uneven.
Only the center of mass covers equal steps; the handle end sometimes swings forward and sometimes back.
The handle end is sometimes ahead of the center of mass and sometimes behind it as the wrench turns.
The dot's path is wavy because the wrench turns while it slides.

why.correct: The center of mass is a mass-weighted average position, so it sits nearer to where more of the mass is. The steel head holds most of the mass.
options: Right: the average is weighted by mass, and the head is heavy.
The middle of the length is the center of mass only when the mass is spread evenly along it; this wrench's mass is not.
Which end leads depends on how the wrench was thrown; the center of mass depends on where the mass is.
Length alone does not set the center of mass; a long, light handle holds little of the mass.

why.correct: The new Σm·x is (0.20)(0.10) + (0.30)(0.50) + (0.70)(0.30) = 0.38 kg·m, so x_cm = 0.38 kg·m ÷ 1.20 kg = 0.32 m. The center of mass moves (0.70/1.20) × 0.60 m = 0.35 m toward the 0 end.
options: Right: recompute the weighted average with the new position.
This moves the center of mass by the full 0.60 m that clamp 3 moved. One clamp carries only 0.70 of the 1.20 kg, so the center of mass moves 0.70/1.20 of that distance.
The total mass is the same, but the center of mass depends on where the mass is, not only on how much there is.
The middle of the stick is the center of mass of the stick itself, which is negligible here; the clamps set the center of mass.

why.correct: For x_cm = 0.50 m with 1.80 kg in all, Σm·x must be 0.50 m × 1.80 kg = 0.90 kg·m. The three clamps give 0.80 kg·m, so the fourth needs 0.10 kg·m: x = 0.10 kg·m ÷ 0.60 kg = 0.17 m.
A uniform stick acts like 0.12 kg at its middle, 0.50 m. Adding mass at 0.50 m pulls the weighted average from 0.67 m slightly toward 0.50 m: (0.80 + 0.06) kg·m ÷ 1.32 kg = 0.65 m.
options: Right: the stick adds mass at its center, below 0.67 m.
Evenly spread mass still has a center of mass, at the middle of the stick, and it shifts the system's average.
The stick's own center is at 0.50 m, below 0.67 m, so it pulls the average down, not up.
The stick's 0.12 kg is small next to the clamps' 1.20 kg, so it moves the center of mass only a little.

why.correct: For a uniform object the center of mass lies on every line of symmetry, so it is where the lines of symmetry cross: the geometric center.
options: Right: uniform and symmetric means the center of mass is on each symmetry line.
Where you start measuring changes the numbers, not where the center of mass is.
A point on the edge is not on the line of symmetry that runs along the long direction.
A uniform sheet has no heaviest corner; its mass is spread evenly.

why.correct: x_cm = (2.0 kg × 0 + 6.0 kg × 0.40 m) ÷ 8.0 kg = 2.4 kg·m ÷ 8.0 kg = 0.30 m, closer to the heavier ball.
Treat each direction on its own: y_cm = (1.0 kg × 0 + 1.0 kg × 0 + 2.0 kg × 2.0 m) ÷ 4.0 kg = 1.0 m.
The ring is symmetric about every line through its center, so its center of mass is at the center, even though no material is there. A center of mass is a position, not a piece of the object.
options: Right: it lies on every line of symmetry, and they all cross at the center.
The center of mass is an average position; it need not be inside the material.
Up and down do not matter to a uniform ring: the top has no more mass than the bottom.
Every object has a center of mass; for a ring it is a point in empty space.

why.correct: When the question is only about where the whole system goes, the parts do not matter and the center of mass stands for the system. When the question is about how the parts move relative to each other, the inside matters.
options: Right: the landing spot depends on how the center of mass moves; the spin does not change that path.
Twisting is about how the parts of the cat move relative to each other, so the structure matters.
This is about how the parts of the bicycle act on each other, so the internal structure matters.
This is about how the legs push and the body moves inside the system, so it cannot be one point.

why.correct: The surroundings are everything outside the chosen system boundary. The cart (with its wheels), the block and the string are inside; Earth is outside.
options: Right: Earth is not part of the chosen system.
The string was chosen as part of the system.
The block was chosen as part of the system.
The wheels are part of the cart, which is in the system.

why.correct: x_cm = (m × 0 + 3m × d) ÷ 4m = 3d/4 before; after, x_cm = 6m × d ÷ 7m = 6d/7. More mass at ball 2 pulls the center of mass toward it, but never past it.
options: Right: recompute the weighted average with 6m.
Doubling one mass does not double x_cm, because the total mass in the denominator also grows. And 3d/2 is beyond ball 2, which no center of mass of two balls can be.
The center of mass depends on the masses as well as the spacing.
These are distances measured from ball 2, and the change goes the wrong way: more mass at ball 2 moves the center of mass toward ball 2.

why.correct: Positions only mean something once there is an origin; then weight each position by its mass, add, and divide by the total mass.
Four objects interact with the sled: the rope pulls it right, the snow rubs on it to the left (friction), the snow pushes up on it (the normal force), and Earth pulls it down (the weight).
options: Right: rope, friction from the snow, normal force from the snow, and weight.
Three leaves one out, usually the normal force: the snow both rubs on the runners and pushes up on them, and those are two separate forces.
A fifth "force of motion" has no agent. Moving does not need its own force; every force on the sled comes from an object touching it or from Earth.
Two forces would leave out the vertical pair: Earth pulls the sled down and the snow pushes it up.

why.correct: A free-body diagram shows forces exerted ON the sled, each labeled with its type and the object that exerts it (the agent). The snow exerts the friction on the sled.
options: Right: type (friction), agent (snow), object (sled).
The sled does push on the snow, but that force acts on the snow, so it belongs on the snow's diagram, not the sled's.
The rope exerts a tension force on the sled, not friction.
Earth exerts the weight on the sled; friction comes from the surface the sled slides on.

why.correct: Velocity is not a force: no object exerts it. It describes the motion, so it can go beside the scene, but never on the free-body diagram.
options: Right: only forces, each with an agent, go on the diagram.
Friction acts precisely because the runners slide on the snow; it stays.
There is no force of motion. A moving object needs no force to keep moving (this unit explains why).
F_N and F_g come from different agents (the snow and Earth) and are different forces; both belong.

why.correct: Take right as positive. The net force is the sum of the horizontal forces: +55 N + F = −30 N, so F = −85 N. Friction is 85 N to the left.

Two objects act on the bucket: the rope pulls up (F_T) and Earth pulls down (F_g). When the velocity stays constant the forces in each direction are equal in size (2.4 shows why), so the arrows are the same length.
options: Right: two forces, equal lengths, because the velocity does not change.
A longer tension arrow would mean a net force upward, which would make the bucket speed up. Rising does not need a larger upward force.
A "lifting force" has no separate agent: the rope is what lifts, and its pull is already F_T.
Earth pulls on the bucket whether it rises or falls, so F_g is always on its diagram near Earth.

why.correct: Weight is the force with which Earth pulls the bucket: F_g = mg = 4.0 kg × 9.8 m/s² = 39 N (39.2 N rounded to two significant figures).
Only objects that touch the bucket can exert contact forces on it, and the rope is the only one attached to it. The hands pull on the rope, not on the bucket.
options: Right: the rope is attached to the bucket and pulls up on it.
The hands touch the rope, not the bucket; their pull reaches the bucket through the rope as tension.
Earth pulls the bucket down, not up.
The sand is part of the bucket-and-sand object; it does not push the object as a whole up.

why.correct: At rest and at a constant velocity the velocity is not changing, so in both cases the rope's pull equals the bucket's weight. The diagram is the same.
options: Right: rest is just a constant velocity of zero.
Moving up at a steady speed needs no extra pull, so stopping does not reduce the tension.
The rope still holds the bucket up; if it pulled with no force the bucket would fall.
Weight is mg; it does not depend on whether the bucket moves.

why.correct: Every force is one object pushing or pulling on another. That is why every force on a free-body diagram has an agent.
options: Right: no interaction, no force.
An object does not carry a force with it; once nothing pushes it, there is no push.
That describes velocity, which is not a force.
That describes mass.

why.correct: Earth pulls the apple down even through empty air. In this course gravity is the only force at a distance; the rest are contact forces.
options: Right: weight is Earth's pull, a gravitational force at a distance.
A rope has to be attached to pull: tension is a contact force.
The floor must touch the box: the normal force is a contact force.
The road must touch the tire: friction is a contact force.

why.correct: A surface pushes perpendicular to itself and away from itself. On a tilted ramp, perpendicular to the surface is tilted 30° from vertical.
options: Right: "normal" means perpendicular to the surface.
The normal force is straight up only when the surface is level.
A push along the surface would be friction, not the normal force.
A surface can only push an object away from itself; it does not pull it in.

why.correct: Take right as positive: F_net = +60 N + (−25 N) = +35 N, so 35 N to the right.
Downward forces: the weight, mg = 5.0 kg × 9.8 m/s² = 49 N, and the hand's 20 N push. The floor's upward push equals their sum: F_N = 49 N + 20 N = 69 N.
Mass is the amount of matter and does not depend on location. Weight is the pull of the body she stands on: mg = 80 kg × 1.6 m/s² = 128 N, about 130 N.
options: Right: same mass, smaller weight.
780 N is her weight on Earth (80 × 9.8); the Moon pulls with a smaller g.
Her mass does not shrink on the Moon; only the pull on it changes.
This swaps the two ideas: mass stays 80 kg, and the weight is smaller.

why.correct: Only objects touching the puck now, plus Earth, exert forces on it. The stick stopped touching it when it was hit.
options: Right: Earth pulls the puck down.
Right: the ice pushes up on the puck.
The stick no longer touches the puck, so it exerts no force on it now.
There is no force of motion: the puck keeps sliding with no forward force at all.

why.correct: A force is an interaction between two objects. The driver pushes the dashboard forward and the seat pushes the driver back; taken together, the car and driver cannot push themselves along. Only a push from something outside, such as the road or a friend, can.
options: Right: an object cannot exert a net force on itself.
The weight points down; a horizontal push is not fighting it. Even a huge push from inside would not move the car.
The dashboard does feel the push; the point is that the seat pushes back on the driver, so the car as a whole gets no net push.
The car does not move at all; the pushes inside it act on its own parts.

why.correct: The two blocks interact by touching, so the forces they exert on each other are a third-law pair: equal in size and opposite in direction, acting on different objects.
options: Right: same size, opposite direction.
The partner force points the opposite way: the small block pushes back on the large one.
Third-law partners are equal in size whatever the masses; the smaller block does not push with a smaller force.
18 N is what is left of the student's 24 N after the 6.0 N, the net force on the 6.0 kg block, not the partner force.

why.correct: The force between the blocks is the one that speeds up the block that is not pushed by the student. Now that block is the heavier one, so the contact force must be larger (18 N instead of 6.0 N). Within each pair the two forces still match.
options: Right: the contact force now accelerates 6.0 kg instead of 2.0 kg.
The student's push is the same, but which block it has to drive through the contact changes, and that changes the contact force.
The lighter block now does the pushing, but how hard it pushes depends on what it must speed up, the 6.0 kg block.
The blocks still touch and still speed up together, so they still push on each other.

why.correct: An internal force is exerted by one part of the system on another part. Both partners of the push between the blocks are internal; the hand and Earth are outside the system, so their forces are external.
options: Right: both blocks are inside the system.
Right: the partner force is also between two parts of the system.
The hand is not part of the system, so its push is external.
Earth is not part of the system, so its pull is external.

why.correct: Each internal force has a third-law partner inside the same system, equal and opposite. Added over the whole system they sum to zero, so only external forces (the push, the weights and the floor) change how the center of mass moves.
options: Right: internal pairs add to zero for the system.
The force between the blocks is 6.0 N, not small; it drops out because it comes in an equal and opposite pair.
Each block feels one side of the pair, so the force acts on both blocks.
The blocks stay in contact and push on each other the whole time.

why.correct: An ideal rope (massless, does not stretch) has one tension along its whole length. It pulls the car forward and pulls the truck backward with the same size of force.
options: Right: an ideal rope pulls with the same tension at both ends, each end toward the rope.
Being pulled does not make one end's tension larger; for an ideal rope the two ends match.
Leading does not change the tension; the rope pulls the truck back as hard as it pulls the car forward.
A rope pulls each object toward the rope: forward on the car, backward on the truck.

why.correct: Third-law partners act on different objects, so they never cancel each other. Whether the truck speeds up depends on all the forces on the truck, including the forward push of the road on its tires, which is larger than the rope's backward pull.
options: Right: equal pulls, and the motion depends on the other forces on each object.
The third law holds whether objects speed up or not; the pulls are equal.
Equal partner forces act on different objects, so they do not cancel; each object can still speed up.
The car pulls back on the rope and the rope pulls back on the truck; towing is an interaction.

why.correct: The partner of "tires on road, backward" swaps the two objects and the direction: "road on tires, forward". That forward push from the road is what drives the truck.
options: Right: swap the agent and the object, flip the direction.
The rope's pull is a different interaction, between the rope and the truck.
Gravity is a different interaction, between Earth and the truck.
This involves the rope, not the road.

why.correct: A tight rope pulls each object it is tied to toward itself, along its length, whatever the motion. An ideal rope has one tension, so the pull on the car and the pull on the truck are equal in size.
options: Right: forward on the car, backward on the truck, same tension.
A tight rope pulls at both ends; a pull at one end alone is impossible for a massless rope.
At each end the rope pulls toward itself: the car is behind the rope, so it is pulled forward.
A rope cannot push; it can only pull along its length.

why.correct: A third-law pair is one interaction: the same two objects, each acting on the other, with the same type of force. Earth-on-ball and ball-on-Earth are both gravity between the same two objects.
options: Right: two objects, each pulling on the other.
Both forces act on the book, from two different agents, so they cannot be partners.
Both forces act on the crate, from the rope and the floor.
Both forces act on the door.

why.correct: Third-law partners act on different objects. The normal force (table on book) and the weight (Earth on book) both act on the book; they are equal here only because the book is at rest. The weight's partner is the book pulling up on Earth.
options: Right: partners never act on the same object.
They are equal in size here, but that does not make them partners.
One points up and one down; the trouble is which object they act on.
Equal and opposite is not enough; partners must also act on different objects and be the same type.

why.correct: The car and the bug interact, so they push on each other with forces of equal size, whatever their masses. The bug is squashed because the same force has a far larger effect on its tiny mass.
options: Right: third-law partners are always equal in size.
A larger mass does not let one side of an interaction push harder.
The bug cannot push harder than it is pushed.
Every interaction is two-sided: the bug pushes back on the car.

why.correct: The block is at rest, so the string pulls up on it as hard as Earth pulls down: F_T = mg = 3.0 kg × 9.8 m/s² = 29 N. An ideal string over an ideal pulley has the same tension all along, so it is 29 N at the floor too.
Each end of the rope is pulled with 150 N, and an ideal rope has one tension along its length: 150 N. The two pulls do not add up to a tension of 300 N.
options: Right: the tension is the pull at each end.
This adds the two pulls; the rope feels 150 N at each end, which is a tension of 150 N.
The net force on the rope is zero, but the rope is still pulled tight; tension is not the net force.
Nothing splits the pull in half; each end feels the full 150 N.

why.correct: Forces cancel only when they act on the same object. The horse's pull acts on the cart and the cart's pull acts on the horse. The cart moves forward if the horse's pull on it is larger than the friction on the cart.
options: Right: partners are on different objects, so they never cancel each other.
Third-law partners are always equal; the horse does not win the pair.
They do not cancel; each acts on a different object.
The cart pulls back on the horse from the moment the horse pulls, even while the cart is at rest.

why.correct: An ideal string is massless and inextensible, so the tension is the same all along it and objects tied to it move together.
options: Right: massless and inextensible.
A string with mass has a tension that changes along it; the ideal model leaves the mass out.
An ideal string does not stretch, so the objects at its ends move together.
No string can push; it can only pull along itself.

why.correct: She pushes the water back; by the third law the water pushes her forward with a force of the same size. That forward push from outside her body is what moves her.
options: Right: the partner force from the water acts on her.
Her own muscles cannot give her body a net push; the push must come from outside.
Empty space does not push anything; the water does.
She pushes the water backward, not forward, and that force acts on the water.

why.correct: The sign is at rest, so the net force on it is zero. Together the cords pull up exactly as hard as Earth pulls down: mg = 5.0 kg × 9.8 m/s² = 49 N.

Vertically, the two upward components balance the weight: 2F_T sin 30° = mg, so F_T = mg ÷ (2 sin 30°) = 49 N ÷ (2 × 0.50) = 49 N. Each cord pulls with 49 N, more than half the weight, because only part of each pull is upward.

The left cord pulls up and to the left, the right cord up and to the right. With equal tensions and equal angles, the sideways parts F_T cos 30° are equal and opposite, so the horizontal net force is zero, as it must be for a sign at rest.
options: Right: equal tensions, equal angles, opposite sideways parts.
Each cord does pull partly sideways; those parts cancel each other rather than having no effect.
The weight points straight down, so it cannot cancel a horizontal force.
The ceiling touches the cords, not the sign; the only forces on the sign are the two cords and Earth.

why.correct: The cords still hold up the same 49 N. Each cord's upward part is F_T sin θ, and sin 15° is smaller than sin 30°, so each cord must pull harder: F_T = mg ÷ (2 sin 15°) ≈ 95 N.
options: Right: a flatter cord needs a larger tension for the same upward pull.
The length of the cord does not set the tension; the angle does.
The total upward pull is the same, but each cord gives less of its tension upward, so the tension rises.
The weight, mg, does not change when the cords change.

why.correct: Each cord is a separate agent, so each gets one whole arrow along its cord, plus the weight from Earth. Components belong in your equations beside the diagram, not on it, and the net force (zero here) is never an arrow.
options: Right: one whole arrow per agent.
Drawing components as extra arrows double-counts each pull; the exam does not accept components on a free-body diagram.
Two cords are two agents and two forces; merging them hides their directions.
The net force is the sum of the arrows, not an arrow of its own, and here it is zero.

why.correct: The push (120 N forward) and the friction (120 N backward) balance, so the net force is zero. The table agrees: the velocity stays 0.80 m/s, constant.
options: Right: balanced forces, constant velocity.
120 N is the push alone; the friction pulls back just as hard.
This adds the sizes of two forces that point in opposite directions.
120 N is the friction alone; the push cancels it.

why.correct: The first law says zero net force keeps the velocity constant, and the data show exactly that: with push = friction = 120 N, the crate keeps moving at 0.80 m/s. A moving object needs no net force to keep moving.
options: Right: balanced forces, steady motion, in the same rows of data.
The change at 3.0 s shows what an unbalanced force does, but it does not test the claim about 0.0 s to 2.0 s.
The crate never stopping is consistent with the claim and with the first law alike, so it does not decide between them.
The mass tells you how hard it is to change the velocity, not whether a net force is needed to keep it.

why.correct: At 150 N the push is larger than the 120 N friction, so the net force is 30 N forward and the velocity grows: 0.80 → 1.55 → 2.30 m/s.
options: Right: an unbalanced forward force speeds the crate up.
Constant velocity needs zero net force; now the forces are unbalanced.
The 120 N push before 2.0 s did not speed the crate up; only a net force does.
The friction stays at 120 N, less than the 150 N push.

why.correct: Once the hands leave the crate the push is gone. The only horizontal force left is the 120 N friction, backward, so the net force is 120 N backward and the crate slows down.
Zero net force means no change in velocity: an object at rest stays at rest, and a moving object keeps the same speed and direction.
options: Right: translational equilibrium means constant velocity.
Things on Earth slow down because friction is a net force; with zero net force nothing slows.
Moving at a constant velocity is also zero net force.
Speeding up is a change of velocity, which needs a net force.

why.correct: Steady speed in a straight line is constant velocity, so the net force is zero: forward and backward forces are equal.
options: Right: balanced horizontal forces.
A larger forward force would make the car speed up.
The forces are there; they just add to zero. Without the road's push the air would slow the car.
The weight is vertical and is balanced by the normal force; horizontal forces balance each other.

why.correct: Translational equilibrium means zero net force, so a constant velocity: same speed and same direction.
options: Right: at rest and staying at rest.
Its speed is increasing, so the forces on it do not balance.
For an instant its velocity is zero, but gravity is still the only force, so its velocity keeps changing.
Its direction changes on the curve, so its velocity changes; the net force is not zero.

why.correct: The bus moves at constant velocity, so it is an inertial frame. The coin already moves forward with the bus and nothing pushes it horizontally while it falls, so it keeps pace with the bus and lands straight below the hand.
options: Right: no horizontal force, so the coin keeps the bus's horizontal velocity.
That would need the coin to lose its forward velocity, which takes a backward force; air resistance is negligible for a coin.
Nothing pushes the coin forward faster than the bus.
At any constant velocity the coin keeps up with the bus; only a change in the bus's velocity would matter.

why.correct: A braking bus is accelerating, so it is not an inertial frame. Seen from the road, the ball simply keeps its velocity (first law) while the bus slows down beneath it. No forward force acts on the ball.
options: Right: the ball keeps its velocity; the bus is the one that changes.
The floor is nearly frictionless for a rolling ball and cannot push it forward while braking.
Air in a closed bus does not push the ball forward.
Inertia is a property of the ball (its mass resisting a change in velocity), not a force on it.

why.correct: Steady speed means zero net force, so the air pushes up exactly as hard as Earth pulls down: F_air = mg = 60 kg × 9.8 m/s² = 590 N (588 N rounded to two significant figures).
The first law holds in an inertial frame, such as the ground or a train at constant velocity. In a speeding-up or braking vehicle, objects seem to lurch with no force on them.
options: Right: the first law holds there.
Objects can move in an inertial frame; they just keep constant velocity when the net force is zero.
Gravity acts in inertial frames too; it is a force with an agent.
A speeding-up observer is not in an inertial frame.

why.correct: For the whole system, the only external force along the string's path that is not balanced is the block's weight, mg = 0.20 kg × 9.8 m/s² = 1.96 N (the cart's weight is balanced by the track; the tension is internal). a = F_net ÷ m_total = 1.96 N ÷ 1.00 kg = 2.0 m/s².
Apply the second law to the cart alone: the only horizontal force on it is the tension, so F_T = Ma = 0.80 kg × 1.96 m/s² = 1.6 N (1.57 N rounded).
The block accelerates downward, so the net force on it points down: its weight must be larger than the string's upward pull. F_T = 1.6 N while mg = 1.96 N.
options: Right: a downward net force on the block means F_g > F_T.
Tension equals the weight only if the block hangs at rest or moves at constant velocity.
Pulling the cart does not make the tension exceed the weight; the block's own motion caps it below mg.
The string stays tight and pulls on the block the whole time; otherwise the cart would not speed up.

why.correct: a = mg ÷ (M + m). Doubling m doubles the top (the pulling weight) but also increases the bottom, from 1.00 kg to 1.20 kg: a = 3.92 N ÷ 1.20 kg = 3.3 m/s², up by a factor of 1.67.
options: Right: the extra mass both pulls harder and has to be accelerated.
It would double only if the total mass stayed the same; the heavier block adds mass to the system.
A larger pulling weight with the same cart gives a larger acceleration.
The total mass grows too, so the gain is less than the gain in the pull.

why.correct: Both ends of the string pull on objects inside the system, so tension is internal. Internal forces do not change the motion of the system's center of mass, so only external forces go into ΣF = m_total a.
options: Right: internal forces drop out for the system.
The tension is 1.6 N, not negligible; it drops out because it is internal.
On the block the tension points up, opposite the weight.
An ideal pulley only turns the string; the tension is still there.

why.correct: As the net force goes 1.0 → 2.0 → 3.0 → 4.0 N, the acceleration goes about 0.5 → 1.0 → 1.5 → 2.0 m/s²: doubling the force doubles the acceleration, so a ∝ F_net.
options: Right: the ratio a ÷ F_net stays about 0.50 per kg.
The acceleration changes from trial to trial, rising with the force.
Quadrupling the force quadruples the acceleration, no more; the relationship is linear.
Inverse proportion would make the acceleration fall as the force rises; it rises.

why.correct: Slope = Δa ÷ ΔF = (2.01 − 0.51) m/s² ÷ (4.0 − 1.0) N = 1.50 ÷ 3.0 = 0.50 kg⁻¹. By the second law a = F_net/m, so the slope is 1/m: 1 ÷ 0.50 kg⁻¹ = 2.0 kg, the cart's mass.
Same 4.0 N, mass 2.0 → 4.0 kg, acceleration 2.01 → 0.99 m/s²: about half. a = F_net/m, so a ∝ 1/m.
options: Right: a is inversely proportional to m at fixed net force.
More mass makes the cart harder to speed up, not easier.
The data show a clear drop, from 2.01 to 0.99 m/s².
A quarter would need a square: a ∝ 1/m², which the data do not show.

why.correct: The second law fixes the direction of the acceleration, not of the velocity: the acceleration points along the net force. If the net force points right while the cart moves left, the cart slows down.
options: Right: speeding up needs the net force along the velocity.
The direction of motion does not set the direction of the net force; a cart can move left while being pushed right.
A net force opposite the velocity slows the cart down.
A constant nonzero net force gives a constant acceleration, so the velocity changes.

why.correct: a = F_net ÷ m = 12 N ÷ 3.0 kg = 4.0 m/s² (a newton is a kg·m/s², so N/kg = m/s²).
First the acceleration: a = Δv ÷ Δt = (15 m/s − 0) ÷ 5.0 s = 3.0 m/s². Then F_net = ma = 1200 kg × 3.0 m/s² = 3600 N (3.6 × 10³ N).
The net horizontal force is 15 N − 6.0 N = 9.0 N forward (the vertical forces balance). a = F_net ÷ m = 9.0 N ÷ 2.0 kg = 4.5 m/s².
Moving up and slowing down means the acceleration points down, so the net force points down: Earth's pull is larger than the cable's.
options: Right: acceleration down, net force down.
A larger pull would speed the elevator up while it rises.
Equal forces would keep the velocity constant.
A cable can only pull up on the elevator; it slows because its pull is less than the weight.

why.correct: The second law, a = F_net/m, ties the acceleration to the net force and the mass only.

variables.name: The net force is doubled, same puck
variables.why: a = F_net/m: doubling the net force doubles a.

variables.name: A puck with twice the mass gets the same net force
variables.why: Twice the mass at the same net force halves a.

variables.name: The puck is already moving fast when the force starts
variables.why: a depends on net force and mass, not on the velocity the puck already has.

why.correct: F_net = ma, so the new net force is (3m)(2a) = 6ma = 6F.
options: Right: both factors multiply.
This divides by 3 instead of multiplying: more mass needs more force for the same acceleration.
This divides the factor for a by the factor for m; the second law multiplies them.
Factors of change multiply, they do not add.

why.correct: An ideal rope pulls both teams with the same tension. The external forces on each team are the rope's pull and the ground's friction on its feet, so the team whose feet get the larger push from the ground has a net force toward its own side.
options: Right: the tension is the same on both teams, so the ground's forces decide.
With a light rope the two teams pull equally hard on it; one cannot pull harder than the other.
Mass matters only through how much grip the feet get; it does not decide the net force by itself.
The rope pulls each team with the same tension.

why.correct: The scale pushes up on the student with 660 N while Earth pulls her down with mg = 588 N. The net force is 72 N up, so she accelerates upward. Starting from rest, that means speeding up on the way up.
options: Right: the normal force exceeds the weight, so the acceleration points up.
At constant speed the scale would read her weight, 588 N.
Slowing down on the way up needs a downward acceleration, so a reading below 588 N.
At rest the scale reads 588 N, her weight.

why.correct: Second law for the student, up positive: F_N − mg = ma, so a = (660 N − 588 N) ÷ 60 kg = 72 N ÷ 60 kg = 1.2 m/s² upward.

The scale reads the normal force, her apparent weight. The gravitational force mg depends only on her mass and Earth's field, so it stays 588 N; the smaller reading means the acceleration points down (the elevator slows as it nears the top).
options: Right: apparent weight changed, the gravitational force did not.
Earth's pull does not change in an elevator; only the scale's push does.
Her mass does not change during the ride.
A downward acceleration can mean slowing down while moving up, which is what happens near the top floor.

why.correct: In free fall both the student and the scale accelerate down at g. Second law for the student: mg − F_N = mg, so F_N = 0. She is weightless: the gravitational force (588 N) still acts, but nothing pushes up on her.

Gravity at the station's orbit is only about 10% weaker than at the ground; it is what keeps the station in orbit. The astronauts feel weightless because they and the station fall together, so the floor pushes on them with no force: zero apparent weight, like the falling elevator.
options: Right: gravity is nearly as strong; the normal force is what vanishes.
That is the effect, zero normal force, not evidence about whether gravity is present.
The air has nothing to do with gravity's strength.
Floating is what the claim is trying to explain, so it cannot test it.

why.correct: The field is the force per kilogram: g = F_g/m = GM/R² = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹)(6.42 × 10²³) ÷ (3.39 × 10⁶)² = 3.7 N/kg (3.73).
F_g = mg_Mars = 300 kg × 3.73 N/kg = 1100 N (1.1 × 10³ N). The lander's mass is the same as on Earth; its weight on Mars is about 38% of its weight on Earth.
The distance in Newton's law is measured from the center of Mars: it goes from R to 2R. F ∝ 1/r², so the force becomes 1/2² = 1/4 of its surface value.
options: Right: double the center-to-center distance, a quarter of the force.
The force falls with the square of the distance, not the distance itself.
The masses are the same, but the distance has doubled.
Gravity reaches far beyond a planet's surface; it weakens but does not vanish.

why.correct: The two forces are a third-law pair from one interaction, so they are equal in size: Gm₁m₂/r² has both masses in it, the same for each. Mars barely responds because its mass is enormous.
options: Right: the same expression gives both forces.
A larger mass does not let one side of an interaction pull harder.
Every mass attracts every other mass; the pull is two-sided.
Both pulls use the same center-to-center distance.

why.correct: F ∝ 1/r²: tripling r divides F by 3² = 9.
options: Right: the square of 3 is 9.
That forgets to square the factor.
Gravity weakens with distance; it does not grow.
Squaring 3 gives 9, not 6.

why.correct: F = Gm₁m₂/r². Doubling both masses multiplies the top by 4; doubling r multiplies the bottom by 4. The factors cancel: F.
options: Right: 2 × 2 ÷ 2² = 1.
This counts only one mass doubling.
This forgets the distance in the bottom.
This forgets that both masses doubled.

why.correct: F = GMm/r² = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹)(5.97 × 10²⁴)(1000) ÷ (1.274 × 10⁷ m)² = 2.5 × 10³ N, a quarter of the 9800 N it would weigh at the surface.
The field is the gravitational force per unit mass, g = F/m. A 1 kg object feels 9.8 N; a 5 kg object feels 49 N. It equals the free-fall acceleration, 9.8 m/s², since N/kg = m/s².
options: Right: force per kilogram.
An object's weight depends on its mass: mg.
Free-falling objects speed up by 9.8 m/s each second; their speed is not constant.
The field is a force per mass, not a density.

why.correct: Gravitational force is proportional to mass (gravitational mass), and resistance to acceleration is proportional to mass too (inertial mass). a = F/m = (10mg)/(10m) = g. Experiments find these two masses equal, which is why everything falls together.
options: Right: 10 times the force on 10 times the inertia.
Ten times the force acts on ten times the mass, so the acceleration is the same.
The gravitational force is mg, so the rock feels the larger force.
The force on the rock is larger, not equal, and it does not fall faster.

why.correct: Down positive: mg − F_N = ma, so F_N = m(g − a) = 55 kg × (9.8 − 2.0) m/s² = 430 N (429 N rounded).
Slowing while moving down is an upward acceleration, so F_N > mg; constant speed gives F_N = mg; slowing while moving up is a downward acceleration, F_N < mg; free fall gives F_N = 0.
The crate stays at rest, so the net horizontal force is zero. Static friction matches the push: 75 N, opposite to it. It is not μ_s F_N; that is only the largest value static friction can reach.
Sliding starts when the push reaches the maximum static friction: f_s,max = μ_s F_N. On a level floor with a horizontal push, F_N = mg = 25 kg × 9.8 m/s² = 245 N. μ_s = 147 N ÷ 245 N = 0.60.
At constant speed the push balances kinetic friction, so f_k = 98 N. μ_k = f_k ÷ F_N = 98 N ÷ 245 N = 0.40.

Once the crate slides, friction drops to the kinetic value, 98 N. A 147 N push gives a net force of 49 N forward, so the crate speeds up at 49 N ÷ 25 kg ≈ 2.0 m/s². That is why things lurch forward once they break free.
options: Right: kinetic friction is smaller than the maximum static friction.
The push equalled the maximum static friction, but kinetic friction is smaller.
Static friction stops acting once the surfaces slide; kinetic friction cannot exceed μ_k F_N.
Kinetic friction is smaller than maximum static friction, not larger.

why.correct: Doubling the mass doubles the normal force (2mg). Both static and kinetic friction are proportional to F_N, so both pushes double: 294 N and 196 N. The coefficients, which depend only on the surfaces, stay the same.
options: Right: friction ∝ F_N, and F_N doubles.
The coefficients stay the same, but the friction forces depend on the normal force, which doubles.
Kinetic friction is μ_k F_N too, so it doubles as well.
More weight presses the surfaces together harder, increasing friction.

why.correct: Take axes along and perpendicular to the ramp. Along the ramp, gravity's part is mg sin θ, down the slope; the crate is at rest, so static friction balances it: f_s = mg sin 25.0° = 20.0 kg × 9.8 m/s² × 0.4226 = 82.8 N, up the slope.
Perpendicular to the ramp nothing accelerates, so F_N balances gravity's part into the ramp: F_N = mg cos 25.0° = 20.0 kg × 9.8 m/s² × 0.9063 = 178 N, less than the weight, 196 N.
Without friction the crate would slide down the slope. Static friction opposes the sliding that would otherwise happen, so it points up the slope, along the surface.
options: Right: it opposes the tendency to slide down.
Friction opposes the tendency to slide, which is down the slope.
Friction acts along the surface, not vertically.
That is the direction of the normal force.

why.correct: Static friction matches mg sin θ, which grows as θ grows. The normal force is mg cos θ, which shrinks. Eventually mg sin θ needs more friction than μ_s mg cos θ can give, and the crate slips: at tan θ = μ_s.
options: Right: sin θ rises and cos θ falls as the ramp steepens.
The normal force falls: a steeper ramp presses less into the crate.
This swaps the two trends.
Both depend on θ, which has changed.

why.correct: In the model used in this course, kinetic friction is f_k = μ_k F_N: set by the surfaces and how hard they are pressed together, not by speed or by area, and it opposes the sliding.
options: Right: f_k = μ_k F_N.
The model treats kinetic friction as independent of speed.
The same normal force spread over a larger area gives the same friction.
It opposes the sliding of the surfaces.

why.correct: Her shoe pushes back on the track and does not slip, so static friction from the track pushes her forward. Friction opposes the sliding the surfaces would otherwise do, not the motion of the person.
options: Right: static friction forward is what speeds her up.
Friction opposes slipping between surfaces; here that means it points forward on her shoe.
Friction acts along the surface, not perpendicular to it.
Static friction acts without sliding; it is what keeps the shoe from slipping.

why.correct: The only horizontal force is kinetic friction, f_k = μ_k mg = 0.30 × 4.0 kg × 9.8 m/s² = 11.8 N. a = f_k ÷ m = μ_k g = 0.30 × 9.8 m/s² = 2.9 m/s². The mass cancels.
The rope pulls partly upward (50 N × sin 30° = 25 N), so the snow pushes up less: F_N = mg − 25 N = 98 N − 25 N = 73 N. Then f_k = μ_k F_N = 0.10 × 73 N = 7.3 N.
Static friction adjusts to whatever value prevents slipping, up to a maximum of μ_s F_N. Its direction opposes the sliding that would otherwise happen, which need not be opposite the velocity.
options: Right: it is often less than its maximum.
Right: no relative sliding at the contact.
μ_s F_N is the maximum, reached only when slipping is about to begin.
A crate riding on an accelerating truck bed has static friction along its velocity.

why.correct: It takes more force to start an object sliding than to keep it sliding, so usually μ_s > μ_k.
options: Right: breaking free is harder than sliding.
Then objects would stop as soon as they began to slide under a steady push.
They differ for most surfaces; a crate lurches forward once it breaks free.
μ_s is a property of the surfaces; it does not vanish, it just stops applying while they slide.

why.correct: The mass hangs at rest, so the net force on it is zero: the spring pulls up exactly as hard as Earth pulls down. That is why the spring force equals mg in this experiment.
options: Right: translational equilibrium.
A stretched spring pulls, but at rest it pulls with exactly mg; a larger pull would accelerate the mass upward.
The whole weight is balanced by the spring's pull; nothing is left over.
At rest the spring must still hold the mass up; otherwise the mass would fall.

why.correct: The stretch is proportional to the force: 0.400 kg is twice 0.200 kg, so the stretch is twice 0.080 m = 0.16 m. With k: Δx = mg ÷ k = 3.92 N ÷ 24.5 N/m = 0.16 m.
Each extra 0.050 kg adds about 0.020 m of stretch, so the stretch is proportional to the force: Hooke's law, F = k|Δx|, a straight line through the origin.
options: Right: equal steps in force, equal steps in stretch, so the stretch is proportional to the force.
Comparing a mass in kg with a length in m means nothing; they are different quantities.
Any spring stretches more under more weight, ideal or not; this does not show proportionality.
Small stretches are not the test; proportionality is.

why.correct: The spring force depends only on how far the spring is stretched: 0.030 m more stretch adds kΔx = 24.5 N/m × 0.030 m ≈ 0.74 N.
options: Right: more stretch, more spring force.
The spring does not know what hangs on it; it responds to its stretch.
Pulling down stretches the spring more, which increases its pull.
That would need an extra stretch of about 0.11 m.

why.correct: Hooke's law: F_s = −kΔx. The spring is compressed, so its end is displaced toward the wall: Δx = −0.15 m. F_s = −(80 N/m)(−0.15 m) = +12 N, away from the wall. A compressed spring pushes outward.
The cart is at rest, so the student's push balances the spring's 12 N push away from the wall: 12 N toward the wall.
options: Right: equal and opposite to the spring force, on the same cart.
Away from the wall is the spring's push; the student must push the other way.
Only the spring's 12 N needs balancing.
At rest means zero net force, but the spring still pushes, so the student must push back.

why.correct: Just after release the only horizontal force is the spring's 12 N: a = F ÷ m = 12 N ÷ 0.50 kg = 24 m/s², away from the wall.

The spring force, kΔx, shrinks as the compression shrinks, so the acceleration shrinks. But it still points the way the cart moves, so the cart keeps speeding up until the spring reaches its relaxed length.
options: Right: a smaller forward acceleration still speeds the cart up.
A shrinking acceleration still points forward, so the speed still grows.
The spring force depends on the compression, which is decreasing.
Speed falls only if the acceleration points opposite the velocity.

why.correct: F_s = −kΔx: the minus sign means the force points opposite the displacement from the relaxed length, back toward it. A stretched spring pulls; a compressed spring pushes.
options: Right: it points back toward the relaxed length.
It points opposite the stretch, back toward the relaxed length.
It grows in proportion to the stretch.
At the same stretch, a smaller k gives a smaller force.

why.correct: Hooke's law: stretch ∝ force. 5.0 N is 2.5 times 2.0 N, so the stretch is 2.5 × 3.0 cm = 7.5 cm.
options: Right: the stretch scales with the force.
That writes the stretch in centimeters as the same number as the force in newtons. This spring stretches 1.5 cm per newton, so 5.0 N gives 7.5 cm.
That doubles the stretch; the force grew by 2.5 times, not 2.
That multiplies the stretch by 5, using the new force alone instead of the ratio of forces.

why.correct: Both pull up with the block's weight, mg. Δx = mg ÷ k, so the stiffer spring stretches less: 50/200 = 1/4 as much.
options: Right: stretch ∝ 1/k at the same force.
The stiffer spring, A, stretches less, not more.
Same force, but different k, so different stretches.
The ratio of the k values is 4, not 2.

why.correct: Two objects act on the block: the spring (touching it) and Earth. The ceiling touches the spring, not the block.
options: Right: the spring pulls up on the block.
Right: Earth pulls down on the block.
The ceiling does not touch the block; its pull acts on the spring.
That force acts on the spring, so it belongs on the spring's diagram.

why.correct: At rest, kΔx = mg, so Δx = mg/k depends on the weight and the spring constant only.

variables.name: The block is replaced by one of twice the mass
variables.why: Twice the weight needs twice the spring force, so twice the stretch.

variables.name: The spring is replaced by a stiffer one (larger k)
variables.why: Δx = mg/k: a larger k gives a smaller stretch for the same weight.

variables.name: The spring and block are moved to a higher shelf in the same room
variables.why: The weight and k are unchanged, so the stretch is unchanged.

why.correct: The period is T = 1/f = 1 ÷ 2.0 s⁻¹ = 0.50 s. In one period the puck goes once around: v = 2πr ÷ T = 2π(0.50 m) ÷ 0.50 s = 6.3 m/s.
The string's pull is the only horizontal force, so it supplies the centripetal net force: F_T = mv²/r = (0.40 kg)(6.28 m/s)² ÷ 0.50 m = 32 N (31.6 N).
With the string gone, no horizontal force acts on the puck. By the first law it keeps its velocity at that instant, which is tangent to the circle, and moves in a straight line.
options: Right: zero net force, constant velocity, along the tangent.
Nothing pushes it outward; there is no outward force. It only looks like it "flies out" because the circle curves away from its straight path.
Going around a circle needs a net force toward the center; without the string there is none.
Any curved path needs a sideways force; with none, the path is straight.

why.correct: Doubling the frequency doubles the speed, and the needed net force is mv²/r ∝ v². 2² = 4, so the tension quadruples.
options: Right: F ∝ v², and v doubled.
The force depends on the square of the speed.
The radius is the same, but the speed doubled.
A faster puck needs a larger inward force, not a smaller one.

why.correct: The puck touches the string and the table, and Earth pulls on it: three forces. The string's pull is the centripetal net force; "centripetal" names a role, not an extra force.
options: Right: only real forces with agents.
This counts the string's pull twice. The centripetal net force IS the tension here; it is not a separate arrow.
There is no outward force with an agent; the puck tends to go straight, which is not a force.
Nothing pushes the puck forward; at constant speed no force acts along the velocity.

why.correct: At the crest the center of the circle is below the car, so the net force must point down: mg − F_N = mv²/r. F_N = m(g − v²/r) = 1200 kg × (9.8 − 144/45) m/s² = 1200 kg × 6.6 m/s² = 7900 N (7920 N).
The net force at the crest points down, toward the center, so the road pushes up with less than mg. Riders feel lighter going over a hill.
options: Right: F_N < mg at the top of a hill.
F_N is larger than mg at the bottom of a dip, where the center is above.
Constant speed on a curved path is still an acceleration toward the center.
The road pushes with zero force only at one particular speed, √(gr).

why.correct: At the greatest speed the road pushes with zero force (F_N = 0), so gravity alone supplies the net force: mg = mv²/r, so v = √(gr) = √(9.8 m/s² × 45 m) = 21 m/s.
At the limit mg = mv²/r: the mass appears on both sides and cancels. More weight means more downward pull, but the car also needs proportionally more force to turn, so the limit speed is the same.
options: Right: m cancels, leaving v = √(gr).
The larger pull is matched by the larger force needed to turn a heavier car.
At the limit the road presses with zero force, whatever the mass.
The extra force needed is matched by the extra weight; the mass cancels.

why.correct: The velocity keeps changing direction, so the object accelerates. That centripetal acceleration points to the center with size v²/r.
options: Right: centripetal acceleration.
Changing direction is a change of velocity, so there is an acceleration.
An acceleration along the velocity would change the speed.
The acceleration points inward; no outward acceleration exists in an inertial frame.

why.correct: The tires do not slide sideways, so the road's sideways grip is static friction, pointing toward the center of the curve. It is the only horizontal force pointing inward.
options: Right: static friction toward the center.
Kinetic friction would mean the tires skid sideways.
On a flat road the normal force is vertical; it balances the weight.
A forward force along the road cannot turn the car; the turning force must point sideways, toward the center.

why.correct: Vertical: F_N cos θ = mg. Horizontal, toward the center: F_N sin θ = mv²/r. Dividing: tan θ = v²/(gr), so v = √(gr tan θ) = √(9.8 × 60.0 × tan 30.0°) = √339 = 18.4 m/s.
Gravity supplies the centripetal net force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v = √(GM/r) = √[(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹)(5.97 × 10²⁴) ÷ (6.80 × 10⁶)] = 7.65 × 10³ m/s. The station's own mass cancels.
Kepler's third law for circular orbits, from GMm/r² = m(2πr/T)²/r: T² = (4π²/GM)r³, so T ∝ r^(3/2). 4^(3/2) = 8.
options: Right: T² ∝ r³, so T ∝ r^1.5.
That assumes T ∝ r; the period grows faster than the radius.
That is the factor for T², not T.
That would be T ∝ √r; the exponent is 3/2.

why.correct: At the top, the car is upside down against the track, so the track pushes it down, toward the center. Gravity also points down. Together they make the centripetal net force: F_g + F_N = mv²/r.
options: Right: both real forces point toward the center at the top.
The track is above the car at the top, so it pushes the car down, not up.
There is no separate centripetal force; it is the sum of gravity and the normal force.
The normal force points down at the top, and there is no separate centripetal force.

why.correct: Turning gives a centripetal part, v²/r, toward the center. Speeding up gives a tangential part along the velocity. The total acceleration is their vector sum, tilted forward of the center.
options: Right: centripetal plus tangential.
Pointing exactly at the center would keep the speed constant.
Along the velocity alone would not turn the car.
Both turning and speeding up are accelerations.
